summaries.gardner: BlackRock is a top dog in asset management with a strong brand (iShares, Aladdin) and a founder-CEO, but it leads a mature industry rather than an emerging one, and its shares fell about 6% over the past year rather than showing Rule Breaker momentum. It fits some of Gardner's traits (leadership, brand, management) better than the 'emerging industry' and 'overvalued' ones.
summaries.buffett: The business is understandable, has a long record (profitable every year, dividends since 2003, diluted EPS up from $19.79 in 2015 to $35.31 in 2025) and a durable scale advantage. Against that, results swing with markets, recent large acquisitions lowered GAAP margins and returns on equity (about 10% in 2025), and at about 26 times trailing GAAP earnings the price offers no obvious discount.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the scale economics of a $15.5 trillion manager that can charge less than smaller rivals and still earn a 47.8% as-adjusted operating margin in Q3 2026. He would weigh this against the fee compression in index products, the political and antitrust controversy over large index-fund holdings and the risk in a recent acquisition spree.
summaries.lynch: BlackRock is a stalwart: a large, well-known company growing faster than usual (revenue +18.7% in 2025 and +25% in the first nine months of 2026) thanks partly to acquisitions. Its P/E of about 20 on as-adjusted and 26 on GAAP trailing earnings is roughly in line with recent adjusted EPS growth, so it is fairly rather than cheaply priced, and it is anything but overlooked by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: BlackRock shows Fisher-style traits: management keeps launching products as old ones mature (iShares, Aladdin, bitcoin ETFs, private markets via GIP and HPS), a strong global distribution machine and long-term thinking under a founder-CEO. Its edge comes from scale and sales reach rather than R&D, and margin trends have been uneven.
summaries.graham: BlackRock passes Graham's size, dividend (paid every year since 2003) and earnings-stability tests, and EPS grew 78% from 2015 to 2025. It fails his price tests: about 30 times three-year average GAAP EPS and a P/E times P/B of roughly 79, far above his 15 and 22.5 limits.
summaries.thiel: BlackRock has a 'monopoly-like' position in scale index management and Aladdin, a strong distribution engine and a durable position, but it does not have technology ten times better than rivals and asset management is a crowded market. It started from a niche (fixed-income risk management) and expanded, which fits Thiel's pattern, but today it is an incumbent rather than a zero-to-one company.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would see a high-quality compounder with strong operating margins and a founder-CEO, riding the secular shift to ETFs and private markets. Valuation (about 18 times forward earnings per StockAnalysis consensus) is reasonable but not cheap, and the business is levered to markets rather than to AI or software platform shifts.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating (Q3 2026 as-adjusted EPS of $15.93, up 38% from $11.55) and analysts are positive, but the share price fell about 6% over the past year, so the price action does not confirm the fundamentals. Its results depend heavily on market levels and liquidity, which a macro investor would watch closely.
summaries.smith: BlackRock is a good company with durable franchises and high as-adjusted margins, but Terry Smith's focus on high returns on capital is only partly met: acquisitions of GIP, Preqin and HPS added goodwill and intangibles and cut GAAP return on equity to about 10% in 2025. The price is not obviously cheap for that return.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, BlackRock's earnings yield is low (trailing GAAP operating income of $9,264M against an enterprise value of about $186B, roughly 5%) and its return on tangible capital is diluted by acquisition goodwill. It would not rank near the top of a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are a high-return business, skilled and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest. BlackRock has a strong franchise and a long-tenured founder-CEO, but reinvestment has recently come through large acquisitions at returns not yet proven, and the stock pays out much of its profit as dividends and buybacks.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple, durable businesses in a temporary, fixable setback at a big discount. BlackRock is simple and durable, but it is not in distress and trades at about 26 times trailing GAAP earnings, so there is little Dhandho-style 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' discount.
summaries.wood: BlackRock is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense, though it is an important player in blockchain through its bitcoin and ether ETFs and tokenized funds. Its core business is a scale incumbent in asset management with falling product costs passed on to clients.
summaries.ackman: BlackRock fits Ackman's preference for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating businesses with dominant positions and high barriers to entry. Concerns are market sensitivity, leverage-free but acquisition-heavy growth, and a valuation that is fair rather than deeply discounted.
summaries.sleep: BlackRock partly embodies Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared': as iShares grows it cuts fees, making it harder for rivals to compete. But its share count has risen because of acquisition-related Subco units, and its returns depend on markets rather than a reinvesting customer flywheel like Costco or Amazon.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies in huge emerging markets; BlackRock is a mature incumbent founded in 1988. It does solve a large problem (saving and investing for retirement at low cost) and its market is huge, but it is not the kind of early-stage opportunity Sequoia sought.
summaries.nash: BlackRock scores well on Nash's quality and growth categories (25% revenue growth in the first nine months of 2026, a 32% trailing GAAP operating margin, low short interest, a founder-CEO) but trips his instant-kill rule because borrowings ($12,744M) exceed cash ($10,492M) and his red-flag rule because of the 2024-2025 acquisition spree and lower GAAP margins. Valuation looks fair rather than compelling.
